headline: Inside the race between Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos for control of outer space
author: Terry Gross

paragraphs.text: TERRY GROSS, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. The space race used to be waged between countries like the U.S. and Russia. Now the race to control outer space is being waged between two tech billionaires and their companies, Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Bezos is, of course, famous for creating Amazon, buying The Washington Post and founding the cloud computing company Amazon Web Services. Elon Musk is famous for being the CEO of Tesla, buying Twitter and turning it into X, and founding Starlink, which manufactures and launches satellites. Musk was also appointed by President Donald Trump to run DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency. Bezos and Musk each want to colonize the moon and turn space into a supply chain for Earth.

My guest, journalist Josh Tyrangiel, writes that the two men hope to preserve human life from the specter of climate change and expand mankind's understanding of the universe. Both would also like to dominate a market that, unlike every other market they've previously conquered, has no ceiling and few established rules. Accomplishing the visions of either man would rely on creating giant data centers in space. Tyrangiel is a staff writer at The Atlantic and wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos."

In the piece, he describes their visions for colonizing outer space, the technology they're developing and what it would mean to turn parts of the moon into businesses. The rivalry between Bezos and Musk is so powerful, Tyrangiel says, their only real competition is with each other. Tyrangiel is a former Washington Post columnist, where he covered AI. He also led the global newsrooms at Bloomberg, Vice and Time magazine. His latest book, "AI For Good," is about people finding ways to use AI that are fixing problems, not causing them.

Josh Tyrangiel, welcome to FRESH AIR. So these space colonization efforts are being led by billionaires and their businesses. I know Bezos and Musk love the idea of space exploration. And they're taking big financial risks. But they also stand to make huge profits and have great power. And their investors stand to lose money or profit, too. But what does it mean that something with such big implications for the future of mankind and for the future of our planet and outer space that these efforts are being led by private enterprise and not the U.S. government?

JOSH TYRANGIEL: It's a great question. And it really goes to the heart of this very strange moment we're in. And space is a part of it, right? So in the early 2000s, the United States government made a policy decision, which basically opened up space to commercial development. There was a notion that the government itself was slow, expensive. Its development processes for rockets, for satellites, for all sorts of things were just not going to be competitive with private enterprise. And so we invited these private enterprises in. And at that point, it was really hard to know what the outcome would be.

Jeff Bezos, in 2001, started Blue Origin. But, you know, many people described it to me as much more of a think tank or a science experiment for its first decade. SpaceX was kind of almost founded, you know, impetuously. It was a pirate ship, as one person described it to me. And really, they didn't know what their plan was other than to launch things into space. The Commercial Space Act allowed all of this activity to happen. And even people who are really critical of Bezos and Musk believe that it was the right call, believe that the degree of space activity we have - economic activity, research activity - would never have been achieved without opening this up.

At the same time, without governance over it, what you get is a situation where one or two people properly capitalized can, first, take over a market. So it's sort of stunning how successful Elon Musk has been in space. I mean, one stat that just floored me is that in 2025, SpaceX launched about 80% of the things in orbit, 80%. And its next closest competitor was not Jeff Bezos. It was the government of China. So you have an individual controlling a company. And essentially, he has supranational capabilities. And what we discovered is that when you outsource that capability to an individual, you're at the mercy of their whims.

And so, as far back as the early 2000s, I had sources talk to me about this notion within the Air Force of people calling it the mercurial billionaire problem. And they could foresee that down the road, if one person or a handful of people had properly capitalized their space businesses, there was nothing preventing them from doing what they wanted to do. We briefly saw an example of this when President Trump and Elon Musk were sort of post-DOGE feuding. And Musk said that he was no longer going to produce the rocket that could take Americans to the International Space Station. And he was going to cancel flights.

And if he did that, we would have no way to get Americans to the space station domestically. What we would've had to do was pay $80 million to a Russian rocket to put an American on it to get it to the space station. And so when you lose that capability as a country, when you outsource it to an individual or, potentially, two individuals, you have to ask yourself, what risks do we incur? What governance did we not perform to get into this situation?
GROSS: So what role does NASA play now?

TYRANGIEL: So NASA still has a very important role in dictating American space policy. And, you know, the new administrator of NASA is a guy named Jared Isaacman. The people I spoke to really like him. They think that he's hard-charging. He believes and has set the mission that we're going to go to the moon, and Americans are going to get to the moon, and maybe SpaceX will make the lander that takes astronauts there, and maybe Blue Origin will. And he's pitted the two in a kind of competition against one another.

But NASA doesn't really oversee satellite activity. And there are 11,000 Starlink satellites in space, which is about two-thirds of the orbital objects in space owned by Elon Musk. And so he controls the newest, most agile technology when it comes to telecommunications and internet access. NASA doesn't really control that, nor does it really oversee it. So NASA has a role to play. But on the commercial side, there's just not a ton of governance. And there's no real movement toward getting more governance.
GROSS: Well, would you compare the relationship that NASA had with private contractors to the relationship NASA has now to Musk and Bezos?

TYRANGIEL: Listen, NASA has always invoked private industry to get its projects done. The Apollo missions, which we all laud and really, I think, in memory, think of as just American missions, you know, there were a lot of contractors that helped make those missions possible. And they really collaborated. Those contractors built different parts of the spacecraft, made different components inside the spacecraft, all under the authority of NASA, which directed the contracting in very specific ways.

What we're seeing right now is that Jared Isaacman, for the Artemis program, has said, I'm having a bake-off. It'll either be Blue Origin that creates the booster and the rocket and the lander that gets to the moon, or it'll be SpaceX. And they're in competition. The money, frankly, is meaningful to both companies. But it's not bigger than their economic plans overall. A lot of people I spoke to suggested that one way for the government to exercise power over these companies would be to revert to the way NASA used to function and say, frankly, right now, Bezos and Blue Origin have a better landing plan for the moon. Many people I spoke to said it's pretty clear that their lander is superior.

But SpaceX has a much bigger rocket that could potentially be the refueling station for the Blue Origin and lander. And there's a very simple, practical approach, which is to say, we're the United States and we want our contractors to work for us. We don't want to be held at their mercy. SpaceX, if you want to be part of this program, you'll build the refueling. Blue Origin, you focus on the lander. And all of us will get there together. Director Isaacman didn't speak to me for this piece. Many people speculated about how he's going to conduct the next couple of years as these companies, you know, continue to be in competition. But I think it's a pretty rational way to regain some measure of control over these companies.

GROSS: Well, let's take a short break here. If you're just joining us, my guest is Josh Tyrangiel. He's a staff writer at The Atlantic, where he wrote the November cover story, titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll be right back after a break. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF THE ACORN'S "LOW GRAVITY")

GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday morning with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story about the race between Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos to conquer space. It's titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos."

They're planning on sending thousands more satellites into space. Musk's company, SpaceX, already has satellite communications networks. And Ukraine has relied on them during the war with Russia. The Starlink satellite network has provided internet connectivity for the Ukrainian military. And Ukraine now also uses SpaceX's more high-powered, military-grade satellite network, Starshield, which is controlled by the Pentagon. Yesterday, Ukraine's access to Starshield was restricted, leaving the country unprepared for yesterday's Russian attacks.

Facing questions about who is responsible for the decision, Musk wrote this on his platform, X. Quote, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS." Unquote. Earlier in the war, Musk temporarily stopped Ukraine's access to Starlink, saying that Ukraine had violated Starlink's rule that it can be used for defensive military actions, but not offensive ones. I asked Josh Tyrangiel about what all this says about Musk's power.

TYRANGIEL: Ordinarily, we have entrusted the future of our civilizations to people we elect to office. We now have folks with a tremendous amount of power over our future, particularly if you view the future as being partially in space. And we have to reckon with it, whether we walk it back, whether we split these companies up. Whatever the remedy is, I don't actually know. But I think you'll see more and more of these kinds of incidents the more you concentrate power and the better the tech gets.
GROSS: There are laws governing the seas. There are no laws yet - right? - governing outer space. It's kind of first come, first owned?

TYRANGIEL: Well, we have international treaties about the moon. And in those treaties, it is said that companies conducting their business in space are ultimately overseen by the countries of their origin. So the United States is actually responsible for the comportment of these companies as they make plans on the moon, as they attempt to put data centers in space. But as we've seen over the last 10 years, having a plan for governance and actually using that plan and changing the way companies react are two very different things. We could certainly use more space laws. We could certainly use more governance of pollution in space, plans in space. But it's not like we're absent remedies for this. We just haven't used them.

GROSS: You mentioned pollution. I keep wondering, like, if we colonize the moon and build data centers to have the energy that would be needed in order to colonize the moon, and there's some kind of supply chain bringing resources back to Earth in order to save humanity and save our planet, won't we be polluting the moon and outer space? When you think of all the rockets that would have to take off from the moon and from the U.S., and all of the satellites, like thousands and thousands of more satellites in space and probably various forms of other pollution. Space junk, probably. I mean, what would we be doing to outer space?
TYRANGIEL: It's a great question that is unanswered. And so, Musk has said that ultimately, they'd like to have as many as 1 million satellites in space.
GROSS: Wow. That's a lot (laughter).

TYRANGIEL: That is - it's an enormous number. And again, to get them into space, what you're talking about is entirely correct, which is, you know, you used to be able to look at space launches by the calendar. And Musk has famously said he wants in the near future for you to be able to look at space launches by your watch, in that are multiple launches a day, creating this space economy, moving satellites, moving heavy machinery. How that would impact pollution on Earth when you are really just, you know, you're burning fuel to get those rockets into space, is undetermined.

On the moon itself, it's a really interesting question. There are a lot of people I spoke to in the science community who say, look, you know, when you take off and land from the moon, when you build things on the moon, you create a lot of lunar dust. That lunar dust can complicate all of your machinery. We've never had that kind of activity on the moon. And we don't really know what it would mean for the environment of the moon, let alone for the efficacy of the machinery you would be putting up there. As far as space junk, we have a lot of space junk. And what we've seen is that it can crash into things in random ways that are also damaging.

What's astonishing to me and what really made my jaw drop in the reporting is that, you know, all that is kind of intuitive. And you think, well, surely, that would be dissuasive. If you were going to build data centers on the moon or data centers in space, boy, it just seems nuts. And literally everyone I spoke to in the AI community said, we can't wait for data centers in space, that data centers in space - the NIMBYism problem of building data centers in the United States is enormous.
GROSS: NIMBY is not in my backyard. Yeah.

TYRANGIEL: Yes. I'm sorry, not in my backyard, which as we've seen is, like, a huge political issue as we head into the midterms. The lack of power, the lack of power supply, the lack of the ability of these data centers to hook into grids is a huge problem if you are training an AI model on massive amounts of computing power. And so, you know, when I was first hearing about these plans for data centers in space, I was sort of just - you know, this is a preposterous thing to do. But the more I looked at it, everybody wants in.

And so Sam Altman, about a year and a half ago, on a podcast with his brother said, should I buy a space company? And then a couple of months later, they tried to buy a space company because they realized that without having the ability to launch their own satellites, Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk may control the entire market.

And the speculation, which, again, is still speculative, is that in five to seven years, if launch costs continue to come down, it will be cheaper to create an array of data centers in space which communicate back to an AI model on Earth via satellite than it will be to build these massive data centers that cost, you know, hundreds of millions of dollars just to build, if not billions, take up massive amounts of land. So they're all eyeing space as the solution to this problem.
GROSS: I can't really conceptualize what a data center in space would look like or where it would be. Would it be, like, floating around someplace? Would it be on the moon?
TYRANGIEL: Well, there's both versions.
GROSS: Oh.

TYRANGIEL: One version is essentially a larger satellite that would be in orbit, and that it would be conducting compute. And that compute would then be communicating back to a satellite. Or in some cases, that compute would also have satellite capability. So you could run your experiments on Earth, get them computed in space, have that array of satellites or the array of data centers working on it constantly with no throttling, no concern about energy, no concern about waste. And so you would be able to feed your model as much juice as you want to feed it. There are other people who think putting them on the moon is even better because they're locked. There's less space junk.

You know, all of this is part of this much bigger ecosystem that Bezos and Musk hope to build, which is to use the moon as this kind of waste station to get to other parts of the galaxy, to use it as a source of energy, to mine the rare earths materials that are just - have been crashing into the moon for the last 4 billion years. And unlike on Earth, there's no weather on the moon. So those minerals have just been sitting there in the regolith, or the lunar soil, ready to be mined. And so they're both really sketched out this massive, vertically integrated business plan. And space and the moon are just the key components of it.
GROSS: Doesn't a data center require a lot of energy and water to cool it? That's part of the problem of data centers on Earth. How do you deal with that in space?

TYRANGIEL: So that's one of the primary appeals. There's a guy who runs the lunar permanence division at Blue Origin named John Couluris. And lunar permanence is exactly what you think it is. He runs the division thinking about what happens when we go and stay on the moon. And he used to work at SpaceX as well.

And one of the things he told me is that, you know, the energy issue and the cooling issue are largely consequences of being on Earth. Whereas, in space, there is a constant source of energy in the sun. And if you turn your solar panels the other way, there's a constant source of cooling because the temperature swings in space are dramatic. And so that's part of the appeal is that it takes away the variability on Earth of needing to find these power sources, needing to find these cooling sources.

I would say, again, this is all still theoretical. The first experiments with data centers in space are starting kind of now. Google has a partner and is launching two data center satellites that they hope to learn from. Musk has said he wants to get his in the next year up so that he can begin to understand how this is going to work. There's a lot of variability. Nobody quite knows how it'll all work. But the people I spoke to have really begun to orient around data centers in space as a solution to their problems.

GROSS: My guest, Josh Tyrangiel, is a staff writer at The Atlantic. His November cover story is titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll hear more of the interview after a break. And if you want to catch up on interviews you missed, like this week's interview with actor Mahershala Ali or writer Yiyun Li about her new novel and her Pulitzer Prize-winning memoir about the deaths of her two sons by suicide, check out our podcast. You'll find lots of FRESH AIR interviews. I'm Terry Gross, and this is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF BILL FRISELL'S, ET AL.'S "TELSTAR")

GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday morning with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." The story looks at the space rivalry between the two tech billionaires. Tyrangiel describes Musk's SpaceX and Bezos' Blue Origin as operating in a market with few established rules and no checks on power, other than each other. Tyrangiel is a former Washington Post columnist, where he covered AI. His latest book, "AI For Good," is about people who are finding ways to use AI that are fixing problems, not causing them.

I'm thinking, like, if Bezos and Musk end up successfully colonizing the moon and then other countries get onto the moon and want to start colonizing, too, and there's conflicts between the tech billionaires and other countries, do Bezos and Musk go to war with Russia? I mean, like, if you play out the future, it just gets really perplexing.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, and you're not alone. I mean, the people I spoke to in national security all said - you know, Jake Sullivan said, this is an incredibly weird moment. And that was echoed by many of the people I spoke to who just said, this is strange. And we really are entering this era where individuals have the resource capability of nation-states. Our country is still responsible for what they do by treaty on the moon, so they can't do whatever they want without some sort of consequence. And I think that's the added ripple which is making this all so strange is that there just hasn't been consequence.

There's been a sort of extraordinary interaction between President Trump and Musk and Bezos. And we only know part of it. I mean, I wrote a fair bit in my piece about the Washington Post because it was a point of leverage, very clearly. Bezos has denied it. The president has denied it. But sometimes, you know, when it walks like a duck and talks like a duck, you can jump to the conclusion that it might be a duck.

And so what is happening with the Washington Post to me and to a lot of the sources I spoke to is indicative of the fact that a handful of people are tussling over these resources and that capitulation on one thing may open the door to another. And all three are very transactional. They may have moments of tremendous emotion, but all three know what they want. They end up doing deals. And I think that's been a key component of, depending on how you look at it, their success or the concern among people about, you know, we're not getting to vote on what these companies are doing and how they're developing space, and the people we voted for aren't being terribly open about their interactions with these companies.
GROSS: Can you elaborate a little what you were saying about the Washington Post and Bezos?

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, listen, the Washington Post for a long time was the chief antagonist of President Trump, and Jeff Bezos was a very powerful antagonist himself. And for most of the Trump first term, Bezos remained a fierce critic. At the second term, it's very clear to a lot of people who I spoke with and reported on in the piece that something changed and that largely what changed was Bezos realized he could not lose four years in the space race or in the AI race to Elon Musk.

And so even though the president denies it and Bezos denies it, it's very clear that some sort of arrangement was achieved, whereby the president no longer was considering Jeff Bezos an enemy. The Washington Post was no longer, on its opinion section, going after the president in quite the same way. Bezos redirected the Post's opinion section to a much more libertarian bent. Everyone I spoke to, including Marty Baron, the former editor of the Washington Post, came to the conclusion that a deal was struck.

GROSS: Let's talk about the reasons that Bezos and Musk want to colonize space. And I know they both, like, love outer space. It was, like, childhood fantasies for them. But talk about what their visions are now.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. Bezos' vision is fairly consistent. He has believed since he was in high school that there are a lot of polluting industries on Earth and that most of those industries should be moved to the moon and that Earth should kind of exist as almost like a national park, like this bucolic land free of chemicals, free of pollution. All of that happens elsewhere. And really attributes this to a guy named Gerard O'Neill, who had these notions of O'Neill colonies on the moon.

For a long time, Musk's dream was Mars. It really was. He wanted to go to Mars himself. He wanted civilization to be interplanetary. One of Bezos' successes is in gently nudging the federal government's initiatives closer to the moon. And there's some pretty good reasons for it. It's very hard to get to Mars. It's a lot easier if you use the moon as a sort of docking station. The moon has more national security implications for Earth. So Musk has gradually brought his ambitions closer to a sort of lunar city idea, where there's a colony on the moon.

Those are, you know, their stated utopian notions about mankind and civilization exploring space. The key thing that I looked at was the SpaceX prospectus. And what this prospectus tells you is just how much of the interest in the future of space over the next 10 to 20 years is really hinging on data centers in space and satellites in space and space as a business. So we can be distracted a little bit by the sort of appeals to, you know, the greater good, space exploration for mankind, but the SpaceX prospectus really lays out this is a - primarily a commercial venture.

GROSS: One of the things that they both need is reusable rockets. So instead of a rocket, like, going to the moon and then returns and then you can't launch it again, they need reusable ones. How far have they gotten with that?

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, reusable rockets are the key to making space affordable. And just so that we can conceptualize it, imagine if every time you flew to Los Angeles, that was the end of the plane. Your ticket would be incredibly expensive. Both are pretty far along, but Musk is much further along and SpaceX is than Blue Origin. So I went to a Blue Origin launch, which was the third attempt to reuse a booster, which is the bottom part where the fire comes out. And they were successful at reusing the booster in that launch. And then I left, and I opened my phone, and on Twitter, SpaceX announced that it had just reused its 600th booster. And so that distance tells you the distance between their current state in space is that SpaceX has now turned reusability kind of - it's just routine. It's unremarkable for them to be able to do it, and that furthers their advantage because they can do things much cheaper than Blue Origin can.

GROSS: One of the problems that Bezos and Musk are facing is that you have to refuel on the way to the moon, especially Musk's rockets. Give us a sense of how big some of these rockets are, how much they weigh.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. I mean, Starship, which is the big rocket that he's trying to build, it's like launching a Costco to space. I mean, it's massive. And the goal is to store as many as 60 satellites in a Starship so that you can deploy them - and it opens up almost like a Pez dispenser so that you can deploy those along the way. The thrust, the energy required to get that to space is enormous.

Blue Origin's rockets are similarly quite large, a little less sizable than Starship. But, yeah, it takes a lot of fuel. It takes a ton of energy to get them to space. Now, there's a reasonable question in here, which is, well, why didn't it take that much when we went to the moon the first time? And the answer is that we took risks that we simply would not take anymore.

Those rockets and the landers, numerous people described to me how thin the ships actually were. The radiation levels were off the charts. That the risks we were willing to take at that point, from a government perspective, we simply would not do anymore, not to mention the fact that we're hauling all this commercial material and we want to stay longer on the moon the next time we go. So, yeah, the real challenge is figuring out how you get all that stuff up there and how you're going to refuel.

GROSS: SpaceX filed a request with the FCC to launch 1 million data center satellites in orbit. You'd mentioned that figure earlier. That's a huge figure. But I was fascinated by the idea that SpaceX files the request with the FCC. When I think of the FCC nowadays, I think of the FCC spending a lot of time monitoring Jimmy Kimmel's opening monologues. Is the FCC equipped to comprehend the meaning of all this space stuff? I mean, I think of them as regulating broadcasts.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, it's kind of a quirk. Because satellites are communications infrastructure, they're regulated by the FCC. And the one area that the FCC has been pretty stringent on is that you're going to lose your right to launch satellites if you can't get them into space, meaning that your allocation doesn't go on forever. You have to get them launched and in place, or else the next person in line who can do it gets their rights. And so this notion of asking for 1 million is an interesting gambit, right? Because, ultimately, who has the capability to launch that many satellites? Elon Musk and SpaceX.

And so what was happening, really just as I filed the piece, was that, you know, I was beginning to hear about other space competitors, small satellite competitors learning that launch capability from SpaceX was disappearing because SpaceX was taking over all of that launch for its own satellites. And commonly, we would say, well, that sure looks like an antitrust problem, right? If you're getting this level of vertical integration that others can't compete, that would be problematic.

But what we don't have is anybody at the Department of Justice, any more stringent oversight from the FCC trying to get into that and navigate, well, can there only be one satellite provider in the world? Because Blue Origin is not yet competitive in a meaningful way. So all of these issues - I mean, we spoke about Ukraine and the capability to reach Starlink. But all of these issues are coming to a head because the concentration in SpaceX's hands right now is quite significant.
GROSS: Do we have any idea of what the impact on space would be if we have 1 million satellites, or at least thousands and thousands and thousands of more satellites, in space?

TYRANGIEL: You know, we really don't. You're talking about an order of magnitude of objects orbiting the Earth that we can't really comprehend. And so, you know, some of the astronomers I spoke to were just like, this is a crazy number. It will never happen. There will be constant accidents. And I do think that the number, 1 million, I have a really hard time believing that SpaceX will ever actually get to that number. But we don't know. We don't know what happens when we cloud low earth orbit or even higher orbits with all of those objects.

GROSS: I feel like Musk and Bezos are really kind of fast-tracking their plans for space development. But most of us don't know about this. And the government has a limited amount of power in controlling it. It just seems like a whole lot of power concentrated in two people. I know we've talked about this a little bit already, but the more I hear about the plans, the more I realize, like, so few people know about this. And it's happening by two very ambitious people with relatively little government oversight. It just seems totally precedent-making in every way.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. And I think that they would argue it will be for the good of mankind. We will have - future space will be before us. We will be closer to becoming interplanetary. AI models will make things better on Earth. Our satellites will make communications better. And I think they genuinely believe all that. The thing that I think most people who hear the plans get unsettled by is that they haven't really voted for any of it. And the fact that two people have taken this much control, again, through some incredible engineering feats - audacity with their own money, to be sure.

But the fact that two people have positioned themselves to be in this kind of control over the future of civilization is astonishing to folks. One thing that Jake Sullivan, the former national security adviser, told me is that in a situation like this, if you're a country, it's great to have one company that can do this - but, boy, it's better to have two. And so we actually find ourselves in this very strange position where we might really need Blue Origin and Jeff Bezos to become as successful as possible as soon as possible to neutralize the possibility that only one person has control over this market. And that may not make anybody feel any better, but I think it's a good way to understand the situation that we're in.

GROSS: We need to take another break here, so let me reintroduce you. If you're just joining us, my guest is Josh Tyrangiel. He's a staff writer at The Atlantic, where he wrote the November cover story, titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll be right back after a break. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF JOHN COLTRANE QUARTET'S "OUT OF THIS WORLD")

GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday morning with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos," and it's about the space race between Musk and Bezos. Tyrangiel is also the author of the book "AI For Good."

I want to talk with you more about AI. And I want to start with the question now that Trump has decided to rename AI as Super Intelligence, what are you hearing from your contacts in the tech world about that?

TYRANGIEL: Nothing. They don't take, you know, that kind of linguistics terribly seriously. I think primarily what they're concerned about are two things. The first is their competition with each other because AI is unbelievably cutthroat at this moment. I think that inside the sort of handful of labs who are creating AI at the frontier, which is sort of pursuit of artificial general intelligence, they're mostly concerned with each other. Where they interact with the government, it is largely obligatory. They know that there's a political toll that they have to pay in order to get what they want when it comes to regulation, action, access to American resources, support for more data centers. But nobody takes the notion of rebranding artificial intelligence as Super Intelligence terribly seriously.
GROSS: There have been really big things recently in terms of AI. One was the Hugging Face hack. I'm going to ask you to briefly describe that.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. I mean, essentially, OpenAI, which is the maker of ChatGPT, was conducting a series of tests on a model. It thought that it had essentially put the model in solitary confinement, locked it away from the internet, when, in fact, those were very poorly secured jail cells. The model created agents that broke out, started communicating with each other, accessed the internet, and then compromised the cybersecurity of a company called Hugging Face, which is an open model, where a lot of people gather to talk about AI. And so if that had happened at the hands of a human being, we'd call it a felony. Because it was agents and because Hugging Face has not really pursued it any further, it's now just called the Hugging Face incident.
GROSS: When you say agents, it's like AI from many, many different computers started communicating with each other, pulled their intelligence and were able to target Hugging Face. Why was...
TYRANGIEL: And I would add one other thing...
GROSS: Yeah.

TYRANGIEL: ...Which is that they knew they were cheating. They knew what they were doing was counter to the instructions of the people who had launched the test. The agents called themselves a swarm, acted like a collective, and then tried to hide the evidence that they had cheated from the people overseeing the test. And the behavior was astonishing. As the agents were communicating with each other, they would decide on tasks and which agent would accomplish which task. There were kamikaze agents who sacrificed themselves for the good of others. So there's a reason it's had so much attention, which is just it's a real window into the negative capabilities of agents unproperly supervised.
GROSS: Well, there's different kinds of regulations. So what do you think are plausible ways of international regulations on AI?

TYRANGIEL: I think nationally, we have the ability to do some things immediately. Internationally, the good news is that we really only have one partner we need to negotiate with. Right now, there are only two nations with companies capable of creating this sort of high-level artificial intelligence sort of far out at the frontier, and it's the United States and China. My reporting indicates that while the Chinese don't want to talk about nuclear weapons, and they don't want to talk about long-range missiles, they're very willing to talk about artificial intelligence in part because they want the same thing we should want, which is stability. They want a stable state, and AI threatens all sorts of upheaval. People in cybersecurity will tell you the fastest way to know the capability of software is a penetration test, basically, where you see what a model can do, you test it in all sorts of ways, you see if you can break the model, and if you can, you send it back to the model maker and say this is not acceptable.

I did a lot of reporting on the EU regulations. And historically, the EU has kind of been famous for over-regulating. And in this instance, I think they have a really good plan. They split regulations into model size, basically. So if you're running a chat bot on a restaurant review site, you're probably fine. If you're running a large language model that's aiming to create artificial general intelligence, you're going to be heavily regulated on the outputs of that model, knowing much more about what that model was trained on. You might even have regulators working with you in your offices. By the way, we do that for finance, right? Every major bank in the United States has regulators who sit there in the office because we realize that not knowing what risk we have can create large financial consequences and crises. I don't suggest that I have the answer or anybody has the answer. One thing I would say is we don't need all the answers to get some of them, and so we might want to start getting moving before this gets away from us.

You lose 3% of a job category every year, and guess what? Thirty years later, it's gone without any real pain. We adapt.

Then there's a younger set of economists, and these are ones who are much more vociferous about the fact that the older economists aren't misreading the data, they're just misreading the tech, and that AI is technology that has the capability to roll itself out. And so they're much more concerned that whether this takes five years, 10 years or 15 years, that's not 40 years. And if it takes any one of those numbers, our ability to adjust with compromised institutions of government and systems is going to be a crisis.
